concept.name: Consistent Hashing

relationships.description: Connects Consistent Hashing to caching in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Consistent hashing assigns data keys to servers in a way that limits how many keys move when servers are added or removed. This helps avoid widespread cache misses and sudden load on databases.
spark.keyTakeaway: Place keys and servers on the same hash ring. Assign each key to the next server clockwise, and use virtual nodes to spread work more evenly.

concept.whyItMatters: With modulo routing such as hash(key) % numberOfServers, changing the number of servers can redirect many keys. In a cache, this can cause a surge of misses and overload the database. Consistent hashing changes assignments only in the affected parts of the ring.
whenToUse: Distributed caches where servers may be added or removed.
Distributed storage systems that partition data across nodes.
Systems that need to spread keys across a changing pool of workers.
whenNotToUse: A single-server system or a small cluster that rarely changes.
Systems where another routing or partitioning strategy already meets the needs.
Workloads that require global transactions across data on many servers without additional coordination.
keyPoints: Hash ring: a circular range of hash values where both keys and servers are placed.
Key assignment: a key belongs to the first server found by moving clockwise from the key's position.
Node change: when a server joins or leaves, only keys in the affected ring segment need reassignment.
Virtual nodes: multiple ring positions assigned to each physical server to improve distribution.
Replication: store copies on distinct physical servers when resilience is required.

examples.title: Adding a cache server
examples.scenario: A cache cluster grows from 9 servers to 10. With modulo routing, many keys may map to different servers because the divisor changed. With consistent hashing, the new server takes over only a portion of the ring.
examples.outcome: Most keys can continue using their existing cache locations, limiting misses and reducing extra database traffic.

examples.title: A server fails
examples.scenario: A server disappears from the ring. Keys assigned to it move to the next available server clockwise.
examples.outcome: Only the affected keys need new owners, though the receiving servers must have enough capacity to handle the added load.

tradeOffs.factor: Limited key movement vs operational complexity
tradeOffs.pro: Adding or removing a server usually affects only part of the keyspace.
tradeOffs.con: The ring and node changes need to be managed consistently by every client or routing service.

tradeOffs.pro: Multiple positions per server help reduce uneven load and support capacity-based weighting.
tradeOffs.con: More virtual nodes increase routing metadata and can add lookup and management overhead.

tradeOffs.factor: Replication vs storage and network cost
tradeOffs.pro: Replicating data across physical servers can improve availability.
tradeOffs.con: Copies consume extra storage and require coordination during writes and node changes.

failureModes.name: Uneven key distribution
failureModes.description: A few servers may receive a much larger share of keys or traffic than others.
failureModes.mitigation: Use virtual nodes, monitor per-node load, and adjust node weights or placement when needed.

failureModes.name: A failed server overloads its successor
failureModes.description: The next server clockwise inherits keys and traffic, potentially becoming overloaded.
failureModes.mitigation: Keep capacity headroom, spread replicas across distinct physical servers, and use controlled failover or rebalancing.

failureModes.name: Different clients calculate different owners
failureModes.description: Clients with inconsistent ring membership, hash functions, or configuration may route the same key to different servers.
failureModes.mitigation: Use a consistent hashing implementation and hash configuration, and distribute membership changes reliably.

failureModes.name: Too few virtual nodes
failureModes.description: With too few positions, physical servers may be distributed unevenly around the ring.
failureModes.mitigation: Choose and validate a suitable virtual-node count based on the number of servers and workload.

failureModes.name: Replication targets virtual nodes instead of machines
failureModes.description: Several replicas may land on different virtual positions belonging to the same physical server, so one machine failure can lose multiple copies.
failureModes.mitigation: Choose replicas on distinct physical servers, not merely distinct virtual nodes.

commonMistakes: Assuming consistent hashing guarantees perfectly balanced traffic without monitoring or virtual nodes.
Treating the 1/N movement estimate as an exact guarantee for every ring and workload.
Using inconsistent hash functions or ring configurations across clients.
Replicating data across virtual nodes without checking that replicas are on distinct machines.
Ignoring the extra capacity required when a node fails and its keys move elsewhere.

sections.content:
## Move only the keys affected by a server change

**Consistent hashing** places both data keys and servers on a circular hash space called a ring. A key belongs to the first server found by moving clockwise from the key's position.

When a server joins or leaves, only keys in the affected ring segment need a new owner. This avoids remapping the entire keyspace as can happen with modulo routing.

- **Hash ring:** the shared circular space of hash values.
- **Key assignment:** move clockwise from the key to find its server.
- **Virtual nodes:** give each physical server multiple positions on the ring to improve distribution.
- **Replication:** keep copies on distinct physical servers when availability requires it.

### Good candidates

- Distributed caches that scale up or down.
- Distributed storage systems that partition data across nodes.
- Workloads where limiting key movement during membership changes is useful.

### Think twice

- A single server or small, stable cluster.
- Systems that need a different partitioning strategy or global coordination.
- Workloads where a node's successor cannot absorb additional traffic.

## Adding a server, step by step

Imagine a cache cluster with nine servers. With modulo routing, adding a tenth server changes the divisor, so many keys may map to different servers. With consistent hashing, the new server is placed on the ring and takes over only the keys in its segment from the next server clockwise.

Most keys keep their existing owners. The keys that move may need to be fetched again or transferred, so the cluster still needs a plan for rebalancing and extra load.

data.title: Consistent Hashing Ring & Virtual Nodes (Minimal Key Remapping)

edges.label: Hash(key)
edges.title: Map Key to Ring Position
edges.description: Compute 32/64-bit hash of the key (e.g., user:4921 -> 0x9A3F) to place it on the circular [0, 2^32 - 1] ring.

edges.label: Clockwise Lookup
edges.title: Route to Next Virtual Node
edges.description: Walk clockwise (binary search over sorted vnode tokens) to the first vnode (e.g., B_v12 at 0xA100) and route to physical Node B.

edges.label: Join (+150 Vnodes)
edges.title: Insert Virtual Nodes on Scale-Out
edges.description: Node D joins and registers 150 interleaved vnodes around the ring, keeping per-node load variance under ~10%.

edges.label: Migrate ~K/N Keys
edges.title: Minimal Key Remapping on Add
edges.description: Only keys falling immediately counter-clockwise of D's new vnodes (~25% of keys) move from A, B, C to D; ~75% stay put (vs. ~75% churn under hash % N).

edges.label: Leave / Fail
edges.title: Graceful Drain or Node Removal
edges.description: If Node D is removed or fails health checks, its vnodes are dropped and only D's ~25% keys fall forward clockwise to their next neighbor vnodes.

edges.label: 75%+ Cache Hit Kept
edges.title: Preserved Cache Locality
edges.description: Unaffected keys continue hitting the exact same shards on Nodes A, B, and C, preventing origin thundering herds during cluster resizing.

data.caption: Consistent hashing with 150–256 virtual nodes per server bounds load skew and limits key movement to ~K/N during node additions or failures, preserving cache hit rates.

sections.content:
## Use virtual nodes to smooth out the ring

A physical server can appear at multiple positions on the ring. These positions are called **virtual nodes**. They help reduce the chance that one server receives too many keys simply because its single position landed in an unlucky spot.

Servers with more capacity can be assigned more virtual nodes, but the system should still monitor actual traffic and resource use. Virtual nodes improve distribution; they do not guarantee perfectly balanced load.

## Fewer moved keys, with coordination overhead

Consistent hashing can limit how much data changes owners during scaling. In return, the system must maintain a consistent ring configuration and handle uneven load, failover, and replication.

A failed server may send extra work to its clockwise successor. Make sure remaining servers have enough headroom, and place replicas on distinct physical machines.

## Before using consistent hashing

- Use the same hash function and ring configuration wherever keys are routed.
- Use virtual nodes if a single position per server creates uneven distribution.
- Monitor key counts, request volume, and resource use per physical server.
- Leave capacity for node failures and controlled rebalancing.
- Place replicas on distinct physical servers, not just distinct virtual nodes.
- Test what happens when a server joins, leaves, or becomes unreachable.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Consistent hashing assigns data keys to servers in a way that limits how many keys move when servers are added or removed. This helps avoid widespread cache misses and sudden load on databases.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Nodes A, B, C applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Node D (Added / Removed).

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Node D (Added / Removed) experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Use virtual nodes, monitor per-node load, and adjust node weights or placement when needed.

questions.prompt: What is the primary engineering trade-off when applying Consistent Hashing in production?

options.text: Balancing throughput and latency against consistency, memory overhead, or operational complexity.
options.explanation: Correct — Consistent Hashing trades bounded resource/coordination cost for predictable behavior at scale.

options.text: Eliminating all network partitions and hardware failures completely.
options.explanation: No software pattern eliminates physical hardware or network partitions; it only bounds their blast radius.

options.text: Replacing all monitoring and SLOs with static configuration.
options.explanation: Observability and SLOs remain essential to verify assumptions under live traffic.
